sections.h2: What is a Nebraska transfer on death deed, and can the owner still sell?
sections.html:
A Nebraska transfer on death deed names a beneficiary who receives the real estate when the owner dies, and the owner keeps full control of the house until then. The rules sit in the 76-34 series of Nebraska statutes, and the key one for the deed itself is 76-3410.

That section requires the deed to contain the elements of an ordinary recordable deed and to say that the transfer to the named beneficiary happens at the transferor's death. It must also carry the statutory warnings and be recorded in the proper county before the owner dies.

While the owner is alive, 76-3414 says the deed does not take anything away from anyone. The owner can still sell or mortgage the house. The beneficiary has no legal or equitable interest, and the property cannot be reached by the beneficiary's own creditors. The beneficiary does not have to be told about the deed, receive it, accept it or pay anything for it, because 76-3411 makes it effective without notice, delivery, acceptance or consideration.

The deed is also revocable. 76-3406 says so even if the deed or another document tries to say otherwise.

sections.h2: Who has to sign a transfer on death deed, and in front of whom?
sections.html:
The transferor signs, or someone signs in the transferor's presence at his or her direction, and at least two disinterested witnesses attest in writing, all before an officer who can administer oaths. That requirement is in 76-3409, which also supplies the form of the officer's certificate.

The sworn language in that form is specific. The transferor declares that he or she signs willingly, is eighteen or older, is of sound mind and is under no constraint or undue influence. The witnesses declare that they watched the transferor sign, in the transferor's presence and hearing, and that to the best of their knowledge those same statements are true. The notary or other officer then certifies under official seal.

The witnesses matter more than they might appear. A challenge to the deed based on missing disinterested witnesses must be filed within ninety days after the transferor's death, or after the last surviving transferor's death if there were several. After that window, 76-3410(c) bars the claim.

sections.h2: What warnings must the deed contain?
sections.html:
Nebraska requires printed warnings in every transfer on death deed, and deeds created after September 3, 2025 carry one more than older ones. The text comes from 76-3410(b).

Warning topicWhat the deed must tell the owner
Inheritance taxThe property stays subject to Nebraska inheritance tax as if the transferor still owned it at death, and late payment carries interest and penalties
Beneficiary liabilityThe beneficiary can be personally liable, up to the value received, for Medicaid reimbursement, and possibly for estate claims, spousal and child allowances and administration costs
Medicaid eligibilityThe Department of Health and Human Services may require the deed to be revoked for the transferor or spouse to qualify or stay qualified
Insurance (deeds after Sept. 3, 2025)Property insurance may end thirty days after the owner's death unless the beneficiary is added to the policy or buys cover

A recorded deed is not invalidated because the wording of a warning is defective. The Medicaid point has its own statute, 76-3421, which confirms that the department can require revocation. Anyone planning for long-term care should ask an elder law attorney how that interacts with their plan before recording.

sections.h2: Where and when is the deed recorded, and what does it cost?
sections.html:
The deed goes to the register of deeds in the county where the property sits, and the statute gives you a thirty-day clock from the date you sign it. It also has to be recorded while the owner is still alive. A deed that is signed and left in a drawer does nothing.

  • Recording fee. The ordinary register of deeds fee under 33-109 is $10 for the first page and $6 for each added page.
  • Stamp tax. None. 76-902 exempts both transfer on death deeds and their revocations from the documentary stamp tax.
  • Transfer statement at filing. Not required when the deed itself is recorded, and not required for an instrument of revocation signed with the original formalities. 76-214 sets that out.
  • Page format. The usual recording layout rules still apply, including a blank three-inch strip at the top of the first page.

The transfer statement comes later, at the owner's death. 76-3412 says a completed statement must be filed when the conveyance becomes effective because of death. At that point 76-2,126 also requires a death certificate to be filed with the register of deeds, with a cover sheet listing the document title, the earlier recording data, the grantor, surviving grantee and legal description.

sections.h2: What happens to the house when the owner dies?
sections.html:
The interest passes to the beneficiary named in the deed, subject to a few rules in 76-3415 that surprise families.

  • Survival. The beneficiary must outlive the owner by one hundred twenty hours, unless the deed sets a different period. A beneficiary who does not is treated as having died first.
  • Several beneficiaries. Unless the deed says otherwise, they take equal undivided shares with no right of survivorship. If one share fails for any reason, it goes to the others in proportion.
  • Existing debts. The beneficiary takes the property subject to all mortgages, liens, contracts and other interests that applied at death.
  • No title warranty. The property passes without covenant or warranty of title, even if the deed says otherwise.
  • Joint owners. If other joint owners survive the transferor, the property belongs to them by survivorship. The deed works only for the last surviving joint owner.
  • Divorce. A divorce, dissolution or annulment after recording revokes the disposition, as provided in section 30-2333.

A beneficiary may also refuse the gift in whole or in part by disclaimer under 76-3416, which points to section 30-2352.

sections.h2: How do you revoke or change a Nebraska transfer on death deed?
sections.html:
You revoke it with a recorded document, and tearing up or writing on the original does not count. 76-3413 states that after recording, the deed cannot be revoked by a revocatory act on the deed itself.

The statute lists four valid instruments:

  • a new transfer on death deed that revokes the earlier one expressly or by inconsistency;
  • a separate instrument of revocation, signed with the same witness and officer formalities as the original;
  • an ordinary deed made during life that revokes it expressly or by inconsistency;
  • an ordinary deed to a bona fide purchaser that does the same.

Most of these must be acknowledged after the deed being revoked and recorded before the owner dies, in the county where the first deed was recorded. A deed to a bona fide purchaser has a longer window: it must be recorded by the later of thirty days after signing or the owner's death.

With more than one transferor, a revocation by one does not affect the others' interests, and a deed from joint owners is revoked only if all living joint owners who signed it revoke.

sections.h2: Selling a house that has a transfer on death deed on it
sections.html:
If the owner is alive, the deed does not stand in the way of a sale. The owner signs a normal deed to the buyer, and 76-3413 lists a deed to a bona fide purchaser as one way to revoke the earlier deed. Section 76-3414 confirms that the owner's right to transfer or encumber the property is untouched.

After the owner's death, the beneficiary who wants to sell usually needs the recorded death certificate and cover sheet in the county records first, so the title shows who now owns the home. A buyer or title company will look for those filings, the stamp tax exemption and any liens that passed along with the property.

Families in that position often live out of state, and the house may be empty and need work. We buy Nebraska houses as-is, so repairs and clutter are not a barrier to a conversation about selling.

faqs.q: Does a Nebraska transfer on death deed avoid probate?
faqs.a: The deed passes the named real estate directly to the beneficiary at the owner's death, which is its purpose under the 76-34 series of Nebraska statutes. The deed does not remove inheritance tax, and the beneficiary takes the property subject to existing liens under 76-3415.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house after signing a transfer on death deed?
faqs.a: Yes. Under 76-3414 the deed does not affect the owner's right to transfer or encumber the property during life. Section 76-3413 also lists a deed to a bona fide purchaser as a way to revoke it.

faqs.q: How many witnesses does a Nebraska transfer on death deed need?
faqs.a: Two or more disinterested witnesses, who sign along with the transferor before a notary or another officer authorized to administer oaths, under 76-3409.

faqs.q: Does a transfer on death deed pay Nebraska documentary stamp tax?
faqs.a: No. Section 76-902 exempts transfer on death deeds and their revocations. The normal recording fee of $10 for the first page and $6 for each added page still applies.

faqs.q: Can Medicaid affect a transfer on death deed in Nebraska?
faqs.a: Yes. The deed must warn that the Department of Health and Human Services may require revocation for Medicaid eligibility, and 76-3421 gives the department that power. The beneficiary can also be liable up to the value received for Medicaid reimbursement.
